title: Pakistan | AML/CFT/CPF Regulatory Compliance
tagline: Apply Pakistan's AML Act, SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, FMU reporting on goAML and targeted financial sanctions with confidence at a conventional bank.
description:
This quest teaches the anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation financing rules that apply to conventional banks in Pakistan. It is based on the **Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010** (as amended), the **State Bank of Pakistan's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations** and risk-based approach guidelines, the **Financial Monitoring Unit's** STR and CTR Reporting Regulations 2025 and goAML guidance, the **Anti-Terrorism Act 1997** and SBP's FAQs on targeted financial sanctions, and the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020.

SBP's regulations require every regulated bank to run an annual, needs-based AML/CFT/CPF training programme for its sponsor shareholders, board, senior and line management and field staff, and to test staff knowledge periodically. Section 7G of the AML Act also requires training programmes. This quest is designed to support that duty for branch, operations, compliance, trade and treasury staff and for managers who oversee them.

Across five stages you follow the compliance team of a fictional Pakistani bank: mapping the law and the authorities, onboarding customers with the right level of due diligence, reporting suspicion on goAML without tipping off, freezing sanctioned funds without delay, and building a programme an SBP inspector would accept.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own AML/CFT/CPF policies, procedures and training records. Always follow your institution's current procedures and the latest SBP and FMU instructions.
audience: Branch, account-opening and teller staff at conventional banks in Pakistan who carry out CDD, handle cash and escalate concerns
Compliance, AML monitoring and sanctions screening staff who review alerts and file STRs and CTRs on goAML
Trade finance, treasury and correspondent banking staff who screen parties and spot proliferation and laundering risk
Line and senior managers, and board members, who approve high-risk relationships and oversee the AML/CFT/CPF programme
Internal auditors and risk managers who test the bank's AML/CFT/CPF controls
outcomes: Explain how the AML Act 2010, the ATA 1997, the UNSC Act 1948, SBP's regulations and FMU's regulations fit together, and who does what
Apply SBP's risk-based approach and CDD, EDD, PEP and beneficial ownership rules to real onboarding decisions
Decide when and how to file STRs and CTRs on goAML, write a usable reason for suspicion, and avoid tipping off
Apply targeted financial sanctions: screen, freeze without delay, report to the FMU and SBP, and handle exemptions and false positives
Keep records for the periods SBP's Regulation 8 requires
Describe the compliance officer's role, the Regulation 13 training programme, board oversight, audit and the sanctions SBP can impose

sessions.title: The Framework: Laws, Offences and Who's Who
sessions.summary: Map Pakistan's AML/CFT/CPF rulebook: the AML Act 2010, the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 and UNSC Act 1948, SBP's regulations and FMU's reporting rules, the money laundering offence, and the roles of SBP, the FMU, NACTA, the Ministry of Interior and MoFA.

Explain the money laundering offence in section 3 of the AML Act and the penalties in section 4

cards.title: Day one at Karakoram Bank
cards.setting: Compliance floor, Karakoram Bank head office, I.I. Chundrigar Road, Karachi. 9:10 am.

lines.text: Your new desk faces the harbour. Your title: Deputy Compliance Officer, AML/CFT/CPF. Your quest: keep dirty money, terror funds and sanctioned names out of Karakoram Bank.
Welcome! I'm Ayesha Siddiqui, Chief Compliance Officer. Five stages lie ahead, and an SBP inspection at the end of the quarter.
Bilal Qureshi, AML analyst. Peshawar has already called. A customer who says he deals in plots brought in a lot of cash this morning.
(on speakerphone from Peshawar) Nadia here, branch manager. He also asked my teller, very casually, who gets to see our reports. That unsettled her.
So which law applies? The AML Act? SBP's regulations? The FMU's new rules? The teller wants a one-line answer.
There isn't a one-line answer, which is why we start here. Before you judge a single deposit, you need the map: the laws, the offence, and who does what.
Stage one is the Statute Hall. Ready to learn the rulebook the way an SBP inspector reads it?

scenes.heading: Parliament sets the base
scenes.narration: It starts with the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010. It creates the money laundering offence, the Financial Monitoring Unit, and the reporting, due diligence and record-keeping duties of every reporting entity, including your bank.

scenes.heading: Sanctions and terrorism laws
scenes.narration: Two more laws sit beside it. The United Nations Security Council Act 1948 brings UN sanctions into Pakistani law, and the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 covers proscription and terrorist financing offences.

scenes.heading: The regulator adds detail
scenes.narration: The AML Act names the State Bank of Pakistan as the AML/CFT regulatory authority for the entities it licenses. Under that power SBP issued its AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, last consolidated in November 2022.

scenes.heading: The FIU sets reporting rules
scenes.narration: The FMU makes regulations on how suspicious and currency transactions are reported. Its Suspicious Transaction and Currency Transaction Reporting Regulations 2025 replaced the 2015 rules.

scenes.heading: Your bank closes the loop
scenes.narration: Finally, your board approves the bank's own AML/CFT/CPF policy, and senior management approves the procedures. That is the layer you will apply every day.

cards.question: A teller in Peshawar asks where a suspicious transaction report actually goes. What is the correct answer?
options: To SBP's Banking Policy and Regulations Department
To the Financial Monitoring Unit, filed by the bank's compliance function
Directly to the nearest FIA office
To NACTA, which handles all financial crime
cards.explanation: Section 7 of the AML Act requires reporting entities to file STRs with the FMU, and section 7(6) makes the FMU the only recipient. SBP supervises whether the bank reports properly, but it does not receive the STRs itself.

cards.title: The money laundering offence (AML Act, sections 3 and 4)
cards.body:
Section 3 makes a person guilty of money laundering if, **knowing or having reason to believe** that property is proceeds of crime, they:

- **acquire, convert, possess, use or transfer** it;
- **conceal or disguise** its true nature, origin, location, movement or ownership;
- **hold or possess it for someone else**; or
- **participate, conspire, attempt, aid, abet, facilitate or counsel** any of these.

Two explanations matter for bankers. Knowledge or intent **can be inferred from the facts**, and the prosecution **does not need a conviction for the predicate offence**. Predicate offences are listed in Schedule I. They include corruption, customs and tax offences, foreign exchange offences and narcotics.

Section 4 sets **rigorous imprisonment of one to ten years**, a fine and forfeiture. Legal persons face higher fines, and their directors, officers or employees who are found guilty can be punished too. (Figures as in the FMU's text of the Act amended to September 2020; check for later amendments.)

cards.title: Which limb of section 3?
cards.prompt: Sort each act into the limb of the money laundering offence it fits best.

items.text: Using bribe money to buy a car in a relative's name and then selling it

Swapping cash proceeds for prize bonds or gold
Issuing fake invoices so illicit funds look like trade receipts

Mislabelling a cash deposit as 'sale of family land' with false papers
Keeping a bag of a cousin's extortion cash at home on his behalf
Letting a friend park suspected kickbacks in your account for a while

cards.title: Real case: Pakistan on the FATF grey list, 2018 to 2022
cards.body:
**What happened.** In June 2018 Pakistan committed to an action plan with the FATF and was placed under increased monitoring, the so-called grey list. The Asia/Pacific Group's mutual evaluation of Pakistan was concluded in 2019. Pakistan left the list in October 2022.

**The cost.** The FMU's summary of the 2023 National Risk Assessment says the listing hurt the financial and non-financial sectors. It cites a study estimating a cumulative fall of about **USD 38 billion** in real GDP, along with lower inflows and remittances and reputational damage.

**What changed for banks.** The AML Act was amended in September 2020. CDD, record-keeping and compliance programme duties moved into the Act itself (sections 7A to 7H), and the STR deadline became 'promptly'. SBP issued its AML/CFT/CPF Regulations in 2020 and updated its risk-based approach guidelines.

**Lesson.** Weak controls at individual banks became a national problem. Every alert you clear carelessly adds to that risk.

*Sources: FMU NRA 2023 summary; SBP RBA Guidelines.*

cards.title: The Peshawar question
cards.setting: Video call between the Karachi compliance floor and Peshawar Saddar branch. 11:40 am.

lines.text: The cash customer, Tariq, came back. He says the money is from selling plots in Hayatabad. No sale deed, no buyer details.
He also mentioned that his cousin 'had some trouble with NAB' and helps him find buyers.
Reason to believe is a low bar in section 3. Nobody has to prove the cousin was convicted of anything.
(joining) Farhan, trade and treasury. Careful, though. Plot sales in cash are common. We can't treat every dealer as a criminal.
Both of you are right. Our job isn't to convict anyone. It's to notice, ask, record and escalate, and never to help hide the money.

cards.title: The cousin's 'business' funds
cards.situation: A long-standing customer asks relationship manager Hamza to receive a large transfer from his cousin's 'business' into his personal account and pay it on to several property sellers the same week. Hamza has read in the local press that the cousin is under a corruption inquiry. The customer is friendly and generates good fee income. What should Hamza do?

choices.text: Process it. The customer is not the one under inquiry, and the bank has known him for years.
choices.outcome: Risky. Section 3 covers anyone who transfers or holds property for another while having reason to believe it is proceeds of crime. Hamza's knowledge of the inquiry gives him that reason. Fee income is no defence.

choices.text: Ask the cousin directly whether the inquiry is about these funds before deciding.
choices.outcome: This may alert the subject that the bank is suspicious, and the answer cannot be relied on anyway. It is better to escalate internally and let compliance decide on further CDD or an STR.

choices.text: Hold off, record his concerns and escalate to compliance under the bank's internal reporting procedure.
choices.outcome: Best. Hamza does not need proof. He records the facts, escalates through the internal channel and lets compliance decide on enhanced due diligence and on whether to file an STR, without warning the customer.

choices.text: Decline politely and say nothing to anyone, so the bank is not involved.
choices.outcome: Declining may be sensible, but staying silent loses information the bank may be required to report. An attempted transaction can itself trigger an STR under section 7. Escalate it.

cards.title: Key terms in Pakistan's AML/CFT law

cards.back: A financial institution or designated business that has STR, CTR, CDD and record-keeping duties under the AML Act. Your bank is one.
Property derived directly or indirectly from a predicate offence or a foreign serious offence.
An offence listed in Schedule I of the AML Act, such as corruption, smuggling, tax crimes or narcotics.
A regulator named in Schedule IV of the Act. For banks, it is SBP (section 6A).
Suspicious transaction report: filed with the FMU when the bank knows, suspects or has reason to suspect that a transaction is tainted.
Currency transaction report: filed for cash transactions at or above the threshold set by the National Executive Committee.
Designated person (listed under the UNSC Act 1948) and proscribed person (under the ATA 1997).
Targeted financial sanctions: the duty to freeze and to make no funds available to DPs, PPs and those acting for them.

cards.question: A prosecutor charges a property agent with money laundering, but the person who handed him the cash has never been convicted of corruption. Under section 3, what is the position?
options: The charge can proceed: a predicate conviction is not required and knowledge can be inferred from facts
The charge fails unless the corruption case is decided first
Only the bank, not the agent, can be charged
The case must move to an anti-terrorism court
cards.explanation: Explanation II to section 3 says a conviction for the predicate offence is not required, and Explanation I lets knowledge or intent be inferred from the facts. Waiting for the corruption case is a common misunderstanding.

cards.title: Your own exposure, and your protection
cards.body:
- **Individuals can be prosecuted.** Section 4 applies to 'whoever' commits the offence, and directors, officers and employees of a guilty legal person can be punished as well.
- **Section 37** makes the people running a legal person answerable when an offence happens with their consent, connivance or knowledge.
- **Good-faith reporting is protected.** Section 12 shields the bank and its staff from civil, criminal or disciplinary proceedings for information they provide in good faith under the Act.
- **Secrecy is no excuse.** Section 7(5) makes the reporting duty override secrecy obligations in other laws or contracts.

cards.title: Stage one: what to remember
items: The AML Act 2010 is the base law; the ATA 1997 and UNSC Act 1948 add terrorism and sanctions duties.
SBP is the AML/CFT regulatory authority for banks and issues the AML/CFT/CPF Regulations under section 6A.
The FMU receives and analyses STRs and CTRs and passes intelligence to investigating agencies.
Money laundering needs only knowledge or reason to believe; no predicate conviction is required.
The NRA 2023 rated banks' inherent vulnerability 'Very High', so your controls matter nationally.

cards.prompt: Think of the last time a customer's explanation for their money did not quite add up. Which layer of the rulebook would have guided you, and who in your bank would you have told?

quiz.question: Which law creates the Financial Monitoring Unit and the money laundering offence in Pakistan?
options: The State Bank of Pakistan Act 1956
The Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010
The Anti-Terrorism Act 1997
The Banking Companies Ordinance 1962
quiz.explanation: The AML Act 2010 defines the offence in section 3 and sets up the FMU in section 6. The ATA 1997 deals with terrorism and proscription, not the ML offence or the FIU.

quiz.question: Under which power did SBP issue its AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for the entities it regulates?
options: The Anti-Terrorism Act 1997
An order of the National Executive Committee
A delegation from the FMU's Director General
Its role as AML/CFT regulatory authority under section 6A of the AML Act
quiz.explanation: Section 6A, read with Schedule IV, names SBP as the AML/CFT regulatory authority for entities it licenses and lets it issue regulations on sections 7A to 7H and on proliferation financing. The FMU makes reporting regulations, not SBP's regulations.

quiz.question: A customer's account receives money he 'holds for a friend'. The bank later learns the friend runs an illegal hundi network. Which limb of section 3 best describes the customer's conduct if he had reason to believe the money was criminal?
options: Concealing his own beneficial ownership
Holding or possessing property on behalf of another person
Failing to file a currency transaction report
Conspiring to commit a predicate offence
quiz.explanation: Section 3(c) covers holding or possessing property for someone else while knowing or having reason to believe it is proceeds of crime. Conspiracy to commit the predicate is a different offence, and CTR filing is the bank's duty, not his.

quiz.question: Which statement about proving money laundering under the AML Act is correct?
options: Intent can be inferred from facts, and no predicate conviction is required
The offence applies only to amounts above the CTR threshold
Only a confession can prove knowledge
The accused must first be convicted of the predicate offence
quiz.explanation: Explanations I and II to section 3 allow knowledge to be inferred from the circumstances and remove the need for a predicate conviction. There is no monetary threshold for the offence.

quiz.question: Which body publishes the consolidated list of persons proscribed under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 that banks screen against?
options: The Financial Monitoring Unit
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs
NACTA
The Securities and Exchange Commission
quiz.explanation: SBP's TFS FAQs point banks to NACTA's website for the consolidated list of proscribed individuals. MoFA handles UN Security Council listings through SROs, a separate list.

quiz.question: The NRA 2023 summary assigned which inherent vulnerability rating to Pakistan's banking sector?
options: High
Very High
Low
Medium
quiz.explanation: The NRA 2023 summary rated banks 'Very High', the top rating among financial sub-sectors. Microfinance banks and exchange companies were rated 'High'.

quiz.question: Branch staff learn that a long-time customer is receiving funds from a cousin under a corruption inquiry and paying them on to third parties. The branch manager says: 'Nothing is proven, so there's nothing to escalate.' Why is this wrong?
options: The law turns on reason to believe or suspect, not proof, so staff should escalate internally
Only SBP inspectors can decide whether funds are suspicious
Escalation is needed only if the cousin has already been convicted
The branch should freeze the account immediately
quiz.explanation: Section 3 uses 'knowing or having reason to believe', and the STR duty in section 7 is triggered by suspicion. Proof is never the test. Freezing is a sanctions tool, not the response to an ordinary suspicion.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the investigating or prosecuting agencies named in the AML Act's definition?
options: The National Accountability Bureau
The Federal Investigation Agency
The Banking Mohtasib
The Anti-Narcotics Force
quiz.explanation: The Act's definition lists NAB, FIA, ANF, two FBR intelligence directorates and provincial counter-terrorism departments. The Banking Mohtasib resolves customer complaints and has no role in investigating money laundering.

quiz.question: A bank officer worries that filing an STR breaches the customer's banking secrecy and could lead to a lawsuit. Which pair of AML Act provisions answers this?
options: Section 4 sets penalties, and section 6 creates the FMU
Section 34 on tipping off, and section 37 on legal persons
Section 7(5) overrides secrecy, and section 12 protects good-faith reporting
Section 7C on records, and section 7E on anonymous accounts
quiz.explanation: Section 7(5) gives the reporting duty effect despite secrecy rules, and section 12 shields reporting entities and staff from civil, criminal or disciplinary action for good-faith reporting. The other pairs deal with different issues.

quiz.question: A new trainee says terrorist financing is just money laundering in reverse, so the same red flags always apply. What is the best correction?
options: TF can use clean money, so links to listed persons and the purpose of funds matter as much as their source
TF is not covered by any Pakistani law that applies to banks
TF only matters for amounts above the CTR threshold
TF is handled entirely by MoFA, so banks need no CFT controls
quiz.explanation: Terrorist financing can be funded with legitimate money such as donations, so screening and the destination and purpose of funds are key. The ATA 1997 and the UNSC Act 1948 apply to banks, and SBP's Regulation 4 sets their TFS duties.

sessions.title: Risk-Based Approach, CDD, EDD, PEPs and Beneficial Owners
sessions.summary: Build the bank's internal risk assessment the way SBP expects, then apply customer due diligence under section 7A and Regulation 2: verify identity, find the real owners, decide between simplified, standard and enhanced measures, and handle PEPs, their family members and close associates.

cards.title: A client from the trade desk
cards.setting: Corporate banking floor, Karakoram Bank, Gulberg, Lahore. 10:00 am.

lines.text: Big win for the trade desk! Zarnab Traders wants to open an account. They import electronics and expect heavy LC volumes.
Who owns it? The forms show 90 percent held by a holding company in Dubai. The directors are two Lahore brothers.
One of them, Kamran, is the younger brother of a sitting provincial minister. But he's a businessman, not a politician.
Under SBP's definition, a PEP's siblings count as family members. That changes the approval route straight away.
And our internal risk assessment rates electronics imports through re-export hubs as higher risk. Did anyone look at that?
That's the Gatehouse. First we learn how the bank decides what 'high risk' means. Then we open the door, or keep it shut, for the right reasons.

cards.title: From national risk to customer risk

scenes.heading: The national picture
scenes.narration: Pakistan's National Risk Assessment tells every bank which crimes and channels pose the biggest threats, such as corruption, hundi and hawala, tax crimes and smuggling.

scenes.heading: The bank's own assessment
scenes.narration: SBP's Regulation 1 requires an entity-level internal risk assessment report. It covers customers, products, services, delivery channels, technologies, geographies and even categories of employees.

scenes.heading: From inherent to residual
scenes.narration: SBP's guidelines describe inherent risk first, then how well the controls work, leaving residual risk. If residual risk exceeds the board's appetite, controls must improve.

scenes.heading: The board signs off
scenes.narration: The report goes to the board for approval with a time-bound action plan. It must be updated when circumstances change or when the national assessment is updated.

scenes.heading: Down to each customer
scenes.narration: The bank's policy then says when simplified, standard or enhanced due diligence applies, and every customer gets a risk profile that is reviewed over time.

cards.title: Building the IRAR (Regulation 1 and SBP's RBA guidelines)

items.label: Identify inherent risks
items.detail: Customers, products, services, channels, technologies, geographies and staff categories.

items.label: Rate likelihood and impact
items.detail: Use a risk matrix to place each risk on a low, medium or high scale.

items.label: Test the controls
items.detail: Assess how well CDD, monitoring, STR/CTR and TFS controls are designed and applied.

items.label: Derive residual risk
items.detail: What remains after controls, compared with the board's risk appetite.

items.label: Board approval and action plan
items.detail: Board approves the IRAR with time-bound fixes and resourcing.

items.label: Keep it live
items.detail: Update when threats change and whenever the NRA is updated.

cards.title: Reading a simple risk matrix
cards.caption: SBP's RBA guidelines suggest a likelihood-and-impact matrix to quantify inherent risk before judging controls.

items.label: Low likelihood, high impact
items.detail: Watch closely; strengthen controls and escalation.

items.label: High likelihood, high impact
items.detail: High risk: EDD, senior approval, tighter monitoring.

items.label: Low likelihood, low impact
items.detail: Lower risk: SDD may be allowed if policy permits.

items.label: High likelihood, low impact
items.detail: Medium risk: standard CDD with active monitoring.

cards.question: Who must approve Karakoram Bank's internal risk assessment report under SBP's Regulation 1?
options: The chief compliance officer alone
The board of directors
The FMU
The head of internal audit
cards.explanation: Regulation 1 requires the IRAR to be presented to the board for approval, with recommendations and a time-bound action plan. Compliance prepares it and audit tests it, but the board owns it.

cards.title: CDD: when and what (section 7A and Regulation 2)
Finding the beneficial owner of a company

steps: Identify and verify the company: name, legal form, proof of existence, governing powers, senior managers and address
Understand the company's business and its ownership and control structure
Identify the natural persons with ultimate effective control through ownership
If that is in doubt or no one controls through ownership, identify who controls it by other means
If still no natural person is found, identify the senior managing official
Take reasonable measures to verify each beneficial owner and record how you did it

cards.prompt: Using SBP's Regulation 2, sort each case by the level of due diligence it needs.

items.text: A product your board-approved IRAR rates low risk, opened by a salaried customer with no red flags
A local pharmacy owner with complete documents and expected turnover that fits the shop
A school teacher opening a current account with an ordinary salary profile
A customer from a country listed under the Counter Measures for High Risk Jurisdictions Rules 2020
The spouse of a serving federal secretary
A trust whose settlor and beneficiaries are unclear and whose funds come from abroad
A charity collecting public donations where the risk is assessed as higher

cards.title: Family member or not?
cards.setting: Small meeting room, Lahore corporate branch. 12:30 pm.

lines.text: Kamran isn't a politician! Why should he need senior management approval?
Because SBP defines a PEP's family members as the spouse, ascendants, descendants and siblings. Kamran is the minister's brother, so he is in scope.
And a nephew wouldn't automatically be a family member under that definition. But he could still be a close associate if he's known to be closely connected.
So what do we actually need? I don't want to lose them.
Senior management approval, source of wealth and source of funds, and enhanced monitoring. Then a proper look at that Dubai holding company. Done well, it protects the relationship too.

cards.back: Someone who holds or held a prominent public function in Pakistan, abroad or in an international organisation. Middle-ranking and junior officials are excluded.
Spouse, lineal ascendants and descendants, and siblings of the PEP.
People with joint ownership or close business ties with a PEP, owners of vehicles set up for a PEP's benefit, or others known to be closely connected.
Before the relationship or transaction, and throughout it, because customers can become PEPs later.
Senior management, to start or to continue the relationship, including when an existing customer becomes a PEP.
Establish source of wealth and source of funds, then apply enhanced ongoing monitoring.

cards.title: Opening Zarnab Traders
cards.situation: Zarnab Traders (Pvt) Ltd wants an import account today. 90 percent is held by a Dubai holding company whose owners are not yet disclosed. Director Kamran is the brother of a sitting provincial minister. Farhan says the client will go to a competitor if the account isn't open by Friday. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Open now on standard CDD. Kamran is not the minister, and the Dubai company is properly registered.
choices.outcome: Poor. Siblings are family members under SBP's definition, so Regulation 5 applies. The beneficial owners behind the Dubai company are also still unknown, and Regulation 2 requires them to be identified.

choices.text: Treat it as EDD: identify the owners behind the Dubai company, get source of wealth and funds, and seek senior management approval before opening.
choices.outcome: Best. EDD under Regulation 2(16)-(17) and the PEP measures in Regulation 5 apply. If the owners cannot be identified, section 7D says do not open the account and promptly consider an STR.

choices.text: Open the account but block debits until the ownership documents arrive.
choices.outcome: Partly right on caution, but verification should normally be finished before or while the relationship is set up, and PEP approval cannot come afterwards. Opening first also gives the client a working account before the risk is understood.

choices.text: Decline because anyone linked to a politician is too risky.
choices.outcome: Too blunt. SBP expects risk-based handling of PEP relationships, not blanket refusal. A refused customer can also appeal to SBP under section 7J, so decisions need to rest on documented risk reasons.

items.label: Identity data
items.right: Plus extra detail and more frequent updates

items.label: Purpose of relationship
items.right: Obtain more detail on the purpose of the relationship and of each transaction

items.label: Money trail
items.right: Establish source of wealth and source of funds

items.label: Approval
items.right: Senior management approval to start or continue

items.label: Monitoring
items.right: Enhanced, with selected patterns reviewed more often

cards.question: A customer's nephew is a sitting senator. The customer runs a joint business with the senator. How should the bank treat the customer?
options: As a family member, because all relatives count
As an ordinary customer, because nephews are excluded
As a PEP in his own right
As a possible close associate, applying EDD and PEP measures if the close connection is confirmed
cards.explanation: Under SBP's definition, family members are the spouse, ascendants, descendants and siblings, so a nephew relationship alone does not qualify. Close business relations with a PEP, though, make someone a close associate, which brings in Regulation 5.

cards.title: Real data and a Karakoram case: charity accounts
cards.body:
**Real data.** The FMU's NRA 2023 summary rated **donations** a 'Very High' source of terrorist financing. It assessed about 6.75 percent of non-profit organisations as high risk, 43.64 percent as medium and 49.61 percent as low.

**SBP's rules (Regulation 6).** Banks apply EDD, including senior management approval, to NGO, NPO, charity and trust relationships where risk is higher. Account titles must match the entity's constituent documents. Signatories and governing body members go through CDD and screening. **Personal accounts may not be used to collect donations.**

**The Karakoram case.** A newspaper advert asks for flood-relief donations to an account at Karakoram's Multan branch. The advert names a welfare society, but the account is in an individual's name. Under Regulation 6, the branch marks the account with a caution and compliance considers an STR. The customer is not told why.

cards.title: When CDD cannot be completed
cards.body:
- **Section 7D(1):** if you cannot complete CDD, do not open the account, start the relationship or carry out the transaction. End any existing relationship, and **promptly consider an STR**.
- **Section 7D(2):** if you already suspect ML or TF and believe that continuing CDD would **tip off** the customer, stop the CDD and **file an STR**.
- **SDD is never allowed** once there is a suspicion of ML, TF or PF (Regulation 2(19)).
- **Write down why.** Customers refused or delayed can appeal to SBP within 90 days (section 7J), so record the risk reasons.

cards.title: Stage two: what to remember
items: Every bank needs a board-approved IRAR that uses the NRA and is kept up to date.
CDD covers identity, beneficial owner, purpose and nature, and ongoing monitoring; verify against reliable sources such as NADRA.
Find the natural person behind a company: ownership first, then control by other means, then the senior managing official.
EDD applies to higher risk, to countries under the 2020 counter-measures rules, and to PEPs with their family and close associates.
If CDD fails, don't open or continue, and consider an STR; if CDD would tip off, stop and file.

cards.prompt: Pick one customer type your team onboards often. Using Regulation 2, what would make you move that customer from standard CDD to EDD, and who in your bank approves that?

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four CDD triggers in section 7A(1) of the AML Act?
options: Entering into a business relationship
Doubts about previously obtained customer data
A suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing
The customer asks for a cheque book
quiz.explanation: Section 7A(1) lists a new business relationship, occasional transactions above the prescribed threshold (for SBP-regulated entities, every occasional customer), suspicion of ML/TF, and doubts about existing data. A cheque book request is not a trigger in itself.

quiz.question: Under SBP's Regulation 1, which statement about the internal risk assessment report (IRAR) is correct?
options: It is approved by the FMU before use
It is a one-time exercise done when the bank is licensed
It covers customers only, not products or employees
It must reflect the NRA and be updated when the NRA is updated
quiz.explanation: Regulation 1 requires the IRAR to take the NRA into account and to be updated when circumstances change or the NRA is updated. It covers customers, products, services, channels, technologies and employee categories, and the board approves it.

quiz.question: SBP's definition of a 'family member of a PEP' includes which of these?
options: A PEP's nephew
A PEP's sister
A PEP's business partner
A PEP's cousin
quiz.explanation: Family members are the spouse, lineal ascendants and descendants, and siblings. A sister qualifies. A nephew or cousin does not automatically qualify, and a business partner would be considered as a possible close associate.

quiz.question: A company customer's shares are held through a chain of trusts and nobody can be shown to control it through ownership. According to Regulation 2, what is the next step?
options: Apply simplified due diligence because ownership is spread
Record the trustee company as the beneficial owner and proceed
Identify the natural persons who control the company by other means
Accept the CEO's signed statement that there is no owner
quiz.explanation: Regulation 2(10) is a cascade: ownership control first, then control through other means, and only if no natural person is found, the senior managing official. A legal entity can never be the beneficial owner, and SDD is not a response to opacity.

quiz.question: A relationship manager is onboarding a low-risk salary account under SDD when the customer asks to route large third-party transfers through it. The RM now suspects layering. What does SBP's Regulation 2 require?
options: Continue SDD because the product was approved as low risk
Stop applying SDD, since it is barred once suspicion arises, and escalate for CDD/EDD and a possible STR
Ask the customer to sign a declaration and continue
Close the account and tell the customer it was flagged as suspicious
quiz.explanation: Regulation 2(19) forbids SDD whenever ML, TF or PF is suspected, and section 7D may require an STR. Telling the customer about the suspicion would risk tipping off, which section 34 makes an offence.

quiz.question: Which measure is specifically required for a PEP relationship under SBP's Regulation 5?
options: Approval from the FMU before opening
A minimum account balance set by SBP
Senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship
Filing a CTR for every transaction
quiz.explanation: Regulation 5 requires senior management approval, establishing source of wealth and funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring. The FMU does not approve accounts, and CTRs depend on cash thresholds, not PEP status.

quiz.question: A customer who could not provide beneficial ownership documents is refused an account. Two weeks later he writes to SBP complaining. Under the AML Act, what is this?
options: An appeal to the AML/CFT regulatory authority, allowed within 90 days under section 7J
A tipping-off offence by the bank
A complaint SBP must reject because CDD refusals are final
A matter only the FMU can decide
quiz.explanation: Section 7J lets a person aggrieved by a reporting entity's delay or failure to complete CDD or start a relationship appeal to the regulatory authority within 90 days, and the authority decides within 60. That is why refusals should be documented.

quiz.question: During onboarding, a teller realises the customer matches a pattern in a recent FMU red-flag circular and believes further questions would alert him. Under section 7D(2), what should the bank do?
options: Ask the customer to explain the red flag in writing
Complete CDD first, then decide later
Stop the CDD process and file an STR
Open the account and monitor it quietly for six months
quiz.explanation: Section 7D(2) says that where suspicion has formed and CDD would tip off the customer, the bank should not pursue CDD and should file an STR. Questioning the customer directly about the red flag risks tipping off.

quiz.question: Which of the following does SBP's Regulation 2 prohibit outright?
options: Opening accounts for foreign nationals
Using NADRA verification for identity
Providing services to legal arrangements
Opening or maintaining numbered accounts
quiz.explanation: Regulation 2(12) bans numbered accounts and transactions on fake identity documents. Foreign nationals and legal arrangements can be banked with proper CDD, and NADRA verification is encouraged.

quiz.question: A welfare society advertises for donations using an account number at your branch. The account is titled in its president's personal name. What does Regulation 6 require?
options: Mark a caution on the account and consider filing an STR, since personal accounts can't collect donations
Nothing, provided the president completed CDD
Freeze the account and notify NACTA
Rename the account after the society without further checks
quiz.explanation: Regulation 6 bars personal accounts for charity collections and requires a caution and consideration of an STR when the account title differs from the soliciting entity. Freezing applies to sanctions matches, not to this mismatch on its own.

sessions.title: STRs and CTRs through goAML, Tipping Off and Records
sessions.summary: Turn an alert into a well-founded suspicious transaction report on goAML, file currency transaction reports on time, protect the confidentiality of reporting under section 34, and keep records for as long as SBP requires.
objectives: Apply the STR test in section 7(1) of the AML Act and the prompt-filing duty in the FMU's 2025 Regulations
Choose between STR-F and STR-A on goAML and write a reason for suspicion the FMU can use
Explain when CTRs are due, what the exemptions are, and who can grant discretionary exemptions
Recognise and avoid tipping off under section 34 of the AML Act and Regulation 13
State the record retention periods in the AML Act and SBP's Regulation 8, and know which one the bank follows

cards.title: The alert that wouldn't go away
cards.setting: AML monitoring room, Karakoram Bank, Karachi. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Tariq again. Over nine days he made cash deposits at three of our Peshawar branches, each one a little under the amount that triggers our branch sign-off.
(on video) Then the money goes out by online transfer to six people who don't look connected. None of them are plot buyers or sellers.
Structuring, then rapid movement to unrelated parties. Has anyone asked the teller what Tariq said?
She logged it. He said, 'If anyone asks, it's family money.' And he wanted to know whether the bank reports deposits to the government.
If we form a suspicion, it goes to the FMU on goAML. Promptly, not whenever we get round to it.
Welcome to the Signal Tower. Today you learn to send a signal the FMU can act on, without the customer ever hearing it.

scenes.heading: Something looks wrong
scenes.narration: An alert fires, or a teller notices something odd: structuring, a story that changes, money that moves straight on. Staff record what they saw and raise it through the bank's internal channel.

scenes.heading: Look at the whole picture
scenes.narration: The FMU's 2025 Regulations expect the bank to examine the available facts, including the customer's background and the possible purpose of the transaction, before deciding whether it is suspicious.

scenes.heading: Decide and document
scenes.narration: Compliance decides whether a suspicion has formed. Either way, the reasons are written down so that an inspector can follow the logic later.

scenes.heading: File promptly on goAML
scenes.narration: Once suspicion forms, the STR goes to the FMU promptly on goAML, with the right report type, indicators, a clear reason for suspicion and supporting attachments.

scenes.heading: Silence and records
scenes.narration: Nobody tells the customer. The bank keeps the report, the acknowledgement and the analysis, and gives the FMU any supporting documents it asks for, promptly.

cards.title: The STR journey at Karakoram Bank

items.label: Observe and record
items.detail: Staff note facts, words and documents at the time.

items.label: Internal report
items.detail: Escalate to compliance through the bank's internal channel.

items.label: Analyse
items.detail: Profile, history, counterparties, background and purpose.

items.label: Decide and document
items.detail: Suspicion formed or not, with reasons on file.

items.label: File on goAML
items.detail: Promptly: STR-F or STR-A, indicators, reason, attachments.

items.label: Follow through
items.detail: Keep the acknowledgement, review the relationship, keep monitoring.

cards.title: STR-F or STR-A?
cards.prompt: Using the FMU's STR guidelines, decide which report type fits each case.

items.text: Structured cash deposits followed by quick transfers to unrelated people
Trade payments far larger than the customer's declared business
Repeated inward remittances to a student account that fund a property purchase
An account opening refused because the identity document appears forged
A law enforcement inquiry about a customer with no suspicious transactions
Adverse media linking a customer to fraud, with no transactions to report yet
A walk-in who abandons a transaction when asked about the source of funds

cards.question: Under section 7(1) of the AML Act, which of these on its own can require an STR?
options: Any cash deposit above the CTR threshold
Any transaction by a foreign national
A transaction with no apparent lawful purpose after the facts are examined
Any account opened online
cards.explanation: Section 7(1)(c) covers transactions with no apparent lawful purpose after examining the facts, including background and purpose. A cash deposit above the threshold needs a CTR, not automatically an STR.

cards.title: The STR duty (section 7 and the 2025 Regulations)
cards.body:
**The test.** A reporting entity files an STR when it **knows, suspects or has reason to suspect** that a transaction, or a pattern it belongs to, whether **completed or attempted**:

- involves funds from illegal activity or is meant to hide proceeds of crime;
- is designed to evade the AML Act;
- has **no apparent lawful purpose** once the facts are examined; or
- involves **terrorist financing**.

**The timing.** The Act requires filing **promptly**, which replaced an older fixed deadline. Under the FMU's 2025 Regulations, once suspicion forms the STR goes to the FMU **on goAML**, and banks must have **risk-based procedures**, such as alerts, red flags and indicators, to detect suspicious transactions promptly.

**Backing.** Section 7(5) overrides secrecy duties. Section 12 protects good-faith reporting. Under section 33, **wilfully failing** to file an STR, or giving false information, is a criminal offence.

cards.title: STR versus CTR
cards.caption: The CTR threshold is set by the National Executive Committee; check the current figure in your bank's procedures.

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Knowledge, suspicion or reason to suspect
items.right: Cash transaction at or above the NEC threshold

items.label: Judgement needed?
items.left: Yes: analysis of facts and purpose
items.right: No: it follows from the amount

items.label: Deadline
items.right: Immediately, no later than 7 working days

items.label: Channel
items.right: goAML

items.label: Confidential?
items.right: Yes: section 34 also covers CTRs

items.label: Record retention (SBP)
items.left: 10 years from completion of the transaction
items.right: 10 years from completion of the transaction

cards.back: The software the FMU uses to receive, analyse and exchange reports. It was developed by UNODC for financial intelligence units.
The FMU says reporting through goAML started on 1 January 2019. Hard-copy CTRs ended that day, and hard-copy STRs ended on 1 January 2020.
For suspicious transactions or financial activity in which funds moved. File one report per subject and add linked parties.
For suspicious activity with no funds moved: attempted transactions, LEA inquiries, adverse media, listed persons with no activity.
Selecting at least one goAML indicator is mandatory. Some, such as 'PEP' or 'adverse media', need a second indicator that explains the suspicion.
Mandatory. Who, what, when and how much, and why it is suspicious, written in chronological, plain language.
What the bank already did, such as blocking or refusing. Mandatory to complete for LEA-inquiry cases and for listed-person cases.

cards.title: 'Did you report me?'
cards.setting: Peshawar Saddar branch, teller counter 3. 2:15 pm.

lines.text: Tariq is back at the counter. He leans in close to the teller, Sana.
'My friend at another bank says you people send names to some government unit. Did you send mine? I can make it worth your while to tell me.'
(watching from the manager's cabin, messaging Karachi) He's pressing Sana right now. What does she say?
Nothing about any report, either way. Section 34 makes disclosure a crime, and the 2025 Regulations repeat the ban.
And the bribe offer goes straight into the file. That's new information for the FMU.

cards.title: The question at the counter
cards.situation: Tariq asks Sana directly whether the bank has reported him and hints at a reward. An STR was filed on goAML yesterday. Sana wants to defuse the situation and keep the customer calm. What should she do?

choices.text: Reassure him: 'Don't worry, we never report regular customers like you.'
choices.outcome: This is a false statement made to keep him comfortable, and it engages directly with the question about reporting. It could also undermine the FMU's analysis. Staff should not discuss reporting at all.

choices.text: Tell him truthfully that an STR was filed, because customers have a right to know.
choices.outcome: This is tipping off. Section 34 bans directors, officers, employees and agents from disclosing, directly or indirectly, that a transaction has been reported. It is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment, a fine or both.

choices.text: Process his normal request, decline politely to discuss internal procedures, and report the conversation and offer to compliance.
choices.outcome: Best. Sana neither confirms nor denies anything and handles the customer as usual. The approach and bribe offer go to compliance, which may file a further STR and review the relationship.

choices.text: Refuse all service and ask him to leave the branch immediately.
choices.outcome: A sudden change in treatment straight after the question can itself signal that he has been reported. Any change to the relationship should be decided by compliance, not at the counter.

cards.title: How long to keep records
cards.caption: Records must allow each transaction to be reconstructed and must be admissible as evidence.

items.label: CDD records after the relationship ends (SBP Reg. 8)
items.detail: ID copies, account opening and KYC forms, account files and correspondence.

items.label: Transaction, STR and CTR records (SBP Reg. 8)
items.detail: Counted from completion of the transaction, including the analysis.

items.label: STR and CTR records under the AML Act, s.7(4)
items.detail: After the report was made.

items.label: Transaction and CDD records under the Act, s.7C
items.detail: SBP's regulation is stricter, so banks follow 10 years.

items.label: Records in litigation
items.detail: Or until the court or authority says they are no longer needed.

cards.question: Karakoram closed a customer's account in 2020. Under SBP's Regulation 8, until when must the bank keep his account opening and KYC records, if there is no litigation?
options: Until 2025, five years after closure, as the Act allows
Until the FMU confirms no STR exists
For as long as the core banking system holds them
Until 2030, ten years after the relationship ended
cards.explanation: Regulation 8 requires CDD records to be kept for ten years after the business relationship ends. Section 7C of the Act sets a five-year minimum, but SBP's stricter rule applies to banks.

cards.title: Handling Tariq's case properly
cards.prompt: Put the bank's actions in the correct order.
steps: The teller records Tariq's words and the deposit pattern at the time
The branch raises an internal suspicious activity report to compliance without alerting him
Compliance reviews his profile, history, counterparties and the purpose of the funds
Compliance documents its conclusion that a suspicion has formed
An STR-F is filed promptly on goAML with indicators, reason and attachments
The acknowledgement and analysis are filed, and the relationship is reviewed and monitored

cards.title: Karakoram case: 'Can we stop CTRs for our biggest client?'
cards.body:
Farhan's wholesale client, a large cash-based distributor, deposits cash every day. Each deposit above the threshold creates a CTR, and Farhan asks compliance to 'switch them off'.

**What the 2025 Regulations say.**

- **Automatic exemptions** apply only to cash transactions with federal or provincial government departments or agencies, local governments, statutory bodies, and payments of utility bills issued by utility entities.
- **Discretionary exemptions** can be granted only by the **FMU's Director General**, with National Executive Committee approval and after consulting the regulator. They cover a 'qualified business customer': one with an established relationship, frequent reportable cash transactions and proven low ML/TF risk.
- The bank must **review exempted customers at least 30 days before the exemption expires**, and must tell the FMU promptly if the information turns out to be false or the customer no longer qualifies.

**Outcome.** Compliance tells Farhan that no one inside the bank can switch off CTRs. If the client qualifies, the bank can apply to the FMU with evidence.

cards.title: Writing a reason for suspicion the FMU can use
cards.body:
- Say **who**: the subject, their profile and the expected activity.
- Say **what**: dates, amounts, channels, counterparties and the pattern, told in **chronological order**.
- Say **why**: the gap between expected and actual activity, and the red flags.
- Mention earlier STRs on the same subject, with their reference numbers and dates.
- Use plain language: no jargon, no unexplained acronyms, no ALL CAPS.
- Make sure the indicators you select match the reason you have written.

cards.title: Stage three: what to remember
items: STR when you know, suspect or have reason to suspect, for completed or attempted transactions, filed promptly on goAML.
CTRs: cash at or above the NEC threshold, filed no later than seven working days; only the FMU can grant discretionary exemptions.
Use STR-F when funds moved and STR-A for activity with no transactions; indicators and a clear reason are mandatory.
Tipping off is a crime under section 34; the ban is also in the code of ethics staff and directors sign at induction.
Banks keep CDD records 10 years after the relationship ends and transaction, STR and CTR records 10 years after completion.

cards.prompt: If a customer asked you tomorrow whether the bank had 'reported' them, what exact words would you use? Practise a neutral reply that neither confirms nor denies anything.

quiz.question: Through which system do banks in Pakistan file STRs and CTRs with the FMU?
options: goAML
The Raast payment system
SBP's electronic Credit Information Bureau (eCIB)
NADRA's verification system
quiz.explanation: The FMU's 2025 Regulations require STRs and CTRs to be filed on goAML, the UNODC-developed FIU system the FMU uses. The other systems serve different purposes.

quiz.question: Under the FMU's STR/CTR Reporting Regulations 2025, when must a CTR be filed?
options: Immediately, and no later than seven working days after the cash transaction
Promptly, once a suspicion has formed
Only when the customer is high risk
Within 30 days of the end of the month
quiz.explanation: Regulation 7 and section 7(3) of the Act set the CTR deadline: immediately, but no later than seven working days. 'Promptly once suspicion forms' is the STR standard, not the CTR one.

quiz.question: A customer abandons a large foreign currency purchase when asked for his CNIC. No money changed hands. Which report type fits on goAML?
options: No report, because the transaction did not happen
CTR, because the amount was large
STR-A, because it is suspicious activity with no completed transaction
STR-F, because foreign currency was involved
quiz.explanation: The FMU's guidelines use STR-A for suspicious activity without completed transactions, including attempted transactions. Section 7(1) of the Act covers attempted transactions too, so 'no report' is wrong.

quiz.question: Compliance concludes on Monday that a customer's transfers are suspicious, but the head of compliance wants to 'batch' STRs and file them at month-end. What is the problem?
options: None, provided all STRs are filed within the same quarter
STRs must be filed promptly once suspicion forms, so batching to month-end breaches the rule
Batching is required by goAML for efficiency
STRs need SBP approval before filing, so the delay is unavoidable
quiz.explanation: Section 7(1) and Regulation 4(2) of the 2025 Regulations require the STR to be filed promptly after suspicion forms. A deliberate delay for convenience is inconsistent with that, and SBP does not pre-approve STRs.

quiz.question: A customer asks his relationship manager whether the bank told the government about his deposits. The RM replies: 'I can't confirm it, but you might want to move your money elsewhere.' What has the RM done?
options: Nothing wrong, because he did not confirm a report
Met his duty to treat the customer fairly
Tipped him off indirectly, which section 34 makes an offence
Made a valid STR disclosure under a group agreement
quiz.explanation: Section 34 bans disclosure 'directly or indirectly' that a transaction has been reported. Hinting that the customer should move his money is an indirect disclosure. There is no group disclosure arrangement here.

quiz.question: Section 34 of the AML Act protects the confidentiality of which reports?
options: Only STRs involving terrorist financing
Both STRs and CTRs
STRs only
CTRs only
quiz.explanation: Section 34(1) prohibits disclosing that a transaction has been reported where an STR or a CTR was filed. Many staff assume CTRs are not confidential; they are.

quiz.question: Where must the ban on tipping off appear, according to SBP's Regulation 13?
options: In the account opening form signed by customers
In the code of ethics signed by employees and directors at induction
Only in the compliance department's SOPs
In the bank's annual report
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(4)(d) requires the prohibition on disclosing STRs to be part of the code of ethics that employees and directors sign when they join.

quiz.question: A bank closed a corporate account in 2018. In 2026, the FIA asks for the account opening documents, and the bank is not involved in any litigation. Under SBP's Regulation 8, what is the position?
options: Records are needed only if an STR was filed
The bank could lawfully have destroyed them in 2023 under section 7C
Only the FMU can ask for these records
The bank should still hold them, since CDD records are kept 10 years after the relationship ends
quiz.explanation: Regulation 8(2) requires CDD records to be kept for ten years after the relationship ends, so until 2028. Section 7C's five-year floor is a minimum. SBP's stricter rule governs banks, and Regulation 8(6) requires prompt replies to LEA and FMU requests.

quiz.question: Which of these cash transactions is automatically exempt from CTR reporting under the 2025 Regulations?
options: Daily cash deposits by a large wholesale distributor
Cash withdrawals by a PEP
Cash deposits by a bank employee
Cash payment of a utility bill issued by a gas distribution company
quiz.explanation: Regulation 7(2) exempts government departments and agencies, local governments, statutory bodies and utility bill payments. A wholesale distributor needs a discretionary exemption from the FMU's Director General, if it qualifies at all.

quiz.question: An analyst files an STR on a PEP and selects only the goAML indicator 'Politically Exposed Person'. Why would the FMU's guidelines consider this inadequate?
options: PEP reports must be filed as CTRs
PEP status alone is not suspicious; another indicator must state the actual suspicion
PEPs must be reported through SBP, not goAML
PEP STRs can only be filed by the CEO
quiz.explanation: The FMU's STR guidelines say the PEP indicator does not express a suspicion on its own. A second indicator, such as high-value cash or activity that does not match declared sources, must explain what is suspicious.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions and Proliferation Financing
sessions.summary: Screen against UN designations given effect by MoFA and domestic proscriptions under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, freeze without delay and without prior notice, report to the FMU and SBP, handle exemptions and false positives, and apply the same discipline to proliferation financing.
objectives: Distinguish designated persons under the UNSC Act 1948 from proscribed persons and organisations under the ATA 1997
Apply SBP's Regulation 4 duties: real-time screening, freezing without delay, no funds made available, and reporting
Handle potential matches, false positives, exemptions and frozen-account transactions correctly
Explain how countering proliferation financing fits into SBP's regulations and the bank's training

cards.title: Two alerts before lunch
cards.setting: Sanctions screening desk, Karakoram Bank, Karachi. 11:20 am.

lines.text: Screening hit on an inward remittance for a Quetta customer. The beneficiary's name is close to a Fourth Schedule entry on NACTA's list.
And my trade desk has an LC for 'industrial valves and controllers' shipping through a transhipment port. The end user's name partly matches a UN-listed entity.
Two different regimes. One is domestic proscription under the ATA, the other a UN designation given effect through MoFA. The clock matters for both.
Branch says it's Friday afternoon, so let's look at it on Monday.
Not in the Frozen Vault. 'Without delay' is generally read as within 24 hours. Let's work through both cases properly.

scenes.heading: UN designations
scenes.narration: When a UN Security Council sanctions committee lists a person or entity, Pakistan gives it effect through orders under the United Nations (Security Council) Act 1948. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues these as SROs. SBP calls them designated persons.

scenes.heading: Domestic proscriptions
scenes.narration: Under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, the government can proscribe organisations (First Schedule) and list persons (Fourth Schedule). NACTA publishes the consolidated list of proscribed individuals. SBP calls them proscribed persons.

scenes.heading: Screen in real time
scenes.narration: SBP's Regulation 4 requires real-time screening of customers and occasional customers, with an effective name-screening system and enough trained staff. Beneficial owners, directors, trustees and signatories are screened too.

scenes.heading: Freeze, don't tip, report
scenes.narration: On a true match, the bank freezes the funds without delay and without prior notice, makes no funds or services available, reports to the FMU, and reports the freeze to SBP within 48 hours.

scenes.heading: Proliferation too
scenes.narration: Since 2020, SBP's regulations explicitly cover countering proliferation financing. UN regimes on weapons of mass destruction use the same freeze-and-report discipline.

cards.title: Designated persons (DP) versus proscribed persons (PP)
cards.caption: Source: SBP Regulation 4 and SBP's FAQs on TFS obligations, issued with MoFA and the Ministry of Interior.

items.label: Legal basis
items.left: UNSC Act 1948 and the UNSC (Freezing and Seizure) Order 2019
items.right: Anti-Terrorism Act 1997: s.11B (organisations), s.11EE (persons)

items.label: Where the list comes from
items.left: MoFA SROs reflecting UN committee listings
items.right: Federal or provincial proscription; NACTA publishes the list

items.label: Notice to the account holder
items.right: No legal requirement, but SBP advises telling the customer the reason

items.label: Exemptions handled by
items.left: MoFA: DG (CT) for terrorism regimes, DG (ACDIS) for proliferation regimes
items.right: Ministry of Interior, or the provincial Home Secretary / Chief Commissioner ICT

cards.title: From screening hit to frozen account

items.label: Screening flags a name
items.detail: Real-time screening of customers, parties and transactions.

items.label: Compare identifiers
items.detail: ID number, date of birth, address and other details; any similarity is viewed with suspicion.

items.label: Potential match
items.detail: Temporary freeze; inform SBP for verification with the Ministry of Interior focal point.

items.label: Confirmed match
items.detail: Freeze without delay and without prior notice; make no funds available.

items.label: Report
items.detail: Frozen assets and attempted transactions to the FMU; the freeze to SBP within 48 hours.

items.label: Notify and record
items.detail: Form-B notice for UN freezes; update the MIS of frozen assets.

cards.question: SBP's FAQs on targeted financial sanctions explain how 'freeze without delay' is generally interpreted. What is it?
options: Within 48 hours
Within seven working days
By the next SBP reporting date
Within 24 hours
cards.explanation: The FAQs cite MoFA's guidelines: 'without delay' generally means within 24 hours. The 48-hour period is the deadline for reporting a freeze to SBP, not for the freeze itself.

cards.title: What the freeze reaches (Regulation 4 and ATA s.11O)
cards.body:
**Who.** Duties apply to DPs and PPs, to entities they own or control directly or indirectly, and to anyone acting on their behalf or at their direction.

**What.** Funds and assets owned or controlled wholly or jointly, directly or indirectly, plus funds **derived** from them. No funds, assets, economic resources or financial services may be made available to them unless the law authorises it.

**Where to look.** Customers and occasional customers, plus the beneficial owners, directors, members, trustees and signatories of entity accounts. Also the bank's own vendors, employees, board members, owners and sponsor shareholders.

**Stakes.** Under ATA section 11O, a natural person who breaches the freeze can face up to **ten years** in prison or a fine, and a legal person a fine of up to **PKR 50 million**. Its directors, officers or employees can also be punished. Section 11O also requires a report within 48 hours of a freeze.

cards.title: Allowed on a frozen account?
cards.prompt: Using Regulation 4 and SBP's TFS FAQs, decide whether each action is allowed on an account frozen under TFS.

items.text: Accepting a salary credit into the frozen account without changing its status
Paying out the monthly amount stated in an exemption SRO
Receiving instalments into the person's pre-existing loan account
Issuing a debit card under an exemption, with controls to keep use within it
Deducting routine service charges not specifically allowed
Letting the customer withdraw last month's unused exempted amount as well
Setting off an overdue loan against the frozen balance
Surrendering the dormant frozen balance to SBP as unclaimed deposits

cards.title: A brother, a director, a remittance

lines.text: The Quetta beneficiary isn't the listed man after all. Different date of birth and CNIC. But he is the listed man's brother.
(on the call) Do we freeze the brother's account too? My team says families stick together.
SBP's FAQ is clear: a family tie alone is not enough. We look for evidence that he acts on behalf of, or at the direction of, the listed person.
What about a director of a listed company? Is his personal account caught?
If he is a member working in the designated entity, the FAQ says his personal accounts are liable to be frozen. He is treated as acting on its behalf.

cards.title: Friday 4:30 pm: a potential match
cards.situation: At 4:30 pm on Friday, screening flags an existing customer whose name, father's name and district match a person newly added to a MoFA SRO. The date of birth is missing from the customer's old record. The branch manager wants to wait until Monday so he can call the customer and ask. What do you do?

choices.text: Wait until Monday and call the customer to confirm his date of birth.
choices.outcome: Poor. Waiting breaches 'without delay', and calling the customer gives prior notice, which Regulation 4 forbids. He could empty the account over the weekend.

choices.text: Place a temporary freeze now, inform SBP for verification with the Ministry of Interior focal point, and document everything.
choices.outcome: Best. SBP's FAQs say a potential match gets an immediate temporary freeze and is passed to SBP for onward verification. If it is confirmed, the freeze stands and reporting follows. If it is a false positive, the bank unfreezes after due diligence and reports to SBP.

choices.text: Block only large debits and let small withdrawals continue until it is verified.
choices.outcome: Partial. Any debit could move funds a designated person controls, and SBP expects the potential match to be frozen. Credits can still come in.

choices.text: Close the account and send the balance to the customer by pay order.
choices.outcome: Very poor. This makes funds available to a possible designated person and destroys the bank's ability to freeze. It could be a criminal breach.

cards.back: Under the AML Act, financing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
SBP's FAQs give examples such as the regimes under UNSCR 1718 and UNSCR 2231.
Regulation 4 applies TFS to persons designated under the UNSC Act, and the regulations have covered CPF since 2020.
Regulation 13 requires special emphasis on TFS for both terrorist financing and proliferation financing.
Handled by the Director General (ACDIS) at MoFA, according to SBP's FAQs.
Mostly trade finance, correspondent banking and treasury, where goods, end users and routes need scrutiny.

items.label: List changes
items.detail: Additions, deletions, amendments or retentions, at no fixed interval.

items.label: Official update
items.detail: A MoFA SRO, or a NACTA list update with an email to SBP-regulated entities.

items.label: Update the screening database
items.detail: Without delay, from the official sources.

items.label: Re-screen
items.detail: Customers, beneficial owners, signatories, staff and vendors.

items.label: Act on results
items.detail: Freeze, unfreeze, report and record.

cards.title: Who to approach
cards.prompt: Match each TFS situation to the authority SBP's FAQs name.

pairs.right: Director General (Counter Terrorism), Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Director General (ACDIS), Ministry of Foreign Affairs

pairs.left: Exemption or verification: Schedule I of the ATA
Exemption or verification: Schedule IV of the ATA
pairs.right: Home Secretary of the province, or Chief Commissioner ICT

pairs.left: Report of a freeze by the bank
pairs.right: SBP within 48 hours, and frozen assets or attempts to the FMU

cards.question: A customer is the son of a person on the Fourth Schedule. There is no information that he acts for his father. What does SBP's guidance say?
options: His account must be frozen because sons are always associates
He must be reported to NACTA for listing
A family relationship alone is not a basis for treating him as an associate
The bank must close his account within 48 hours
cards.explanation: SBP's FAQ 13 says a person cannot be penalised merely for a family relationship with a DP or PP. The bank should still screen and use its own analysis to spot anyone acting on their behalf.

cards.title: Real data: how terrorism is financed in Pakistan (NRA 2023)
cards.body:
The FMU's summary of the National Risk Assessment 2023 gives trainees a clear picture of where to look.

- **Sources rated 'Very High':** donations and extortion. Narcotics trafficking and cash smuggling were rated 'High'.
- **Channels rated 'Very High':** cash and cash couriers, and illegal money value transfer services (hundi and hawala). **Banking** and **branchless banking** were rated 'High'.
- **Proscribed organisations:** 78 under the ATA. The NRA found 41 terrorist organisations active to varying degrees and rated 4 of those assessed as 'Very High' risk.

**What it means at Karakoram.** Charity collections, cash-heavy accounts and remittance beneficiaries deserve the closest screening and monitoring. Branchless and digital channels are not low risk just because the amounts are small.

cards.title: Proliferation red flags at the trade desk
cards.body:
SBP has not given banks a fixed checklist here, so use judgement and the bank's procedures.

- Goods described vaguely, or technical items that do not fit the customer's business.
- Shipping routes through transhipment hubs with no clear commercial reason.
- End users or consignees that are new, hard to verify or linked to listed parties.
- Pressure to skip documents, or last-minute changes to parties or routes.
- Payment from third parties with no visible link to the trade.

Screen **every party**: applicant, beneficiary, banks, shipping line, vessel, consignee and end user.

cards.title: Stage four: what to remember
items: DPs come from UN listings through MoFA SROs under the UNSC Act; PPs come from proscription under the ATA 1997, with NACTA publishing the list.
Freeze without delay (generally within 24 hours) and without prior notice, and make no funds or services available.
Report frozen assets and attempted transactions to the FMU, and report the freeze to SBP within 48 hours.
A potential match gets a temporary freeze and verification through SBP; false positives are unfrozen only after due diligence.
Family ties alone don't make someone an associate; acting for or at the direction of a listed person does.

cards.prompt: Where in your daily work could a listed person or their agent reach the bank without being screened: a third-party payment, a new signatory, a vendor? What would you change?

quiz.question: Under SBP's Regulation 4, how must banks screen customers and occasional customers against sanctions lists?
options: Once a year at account review
In real time, using an effective name-screening solution and trained staff
Only when MoFA sends a written instruction to the bank
Only when a customer is rated high risk
quiz.explanation: Regulation 4(3) requires real-time screening with an effective name-screening solution and enough trained resources. Periodic or risk-only screening would miss listed persons.

quiz.question: Within what period must a bank report a TFS freeze to SBP under Regulation 4?
options: At the next quarterly return
Within 48 hours of the freeze
Within 24 hours of the listing
Within seven working days
quiz.explanation: Regulation 4(7)(c) requires the freeze to be reported to SBP within 48 hours. Twenty-four hours is how 'without delay' is generally read for the freeze itself.

quiz.question: Which notice must a bank issue to an account holder affected by a freeze under the UNSC Act 1948?
options: A Form-B notice for every freeze, including ATA freezes
A notice in Form-B of the UNSC (Freezing and Seizure) Order 2019
A tipping-off waiver signed by the CEO
No notice at all, because freezing must be secret
quiz.explanation: Regulation 4(7)(d) requires a Form-B notice for UN freezes. SBP's FAQ says it is not legally required for ATA freezes, although the bank is advised to tell the customer the reason.

quiz.question: A listed company's director, who works in the company, holds a personal savings account with your bank. According to SBP's FAQs, what applies?
options: His personal accounts are liable to be frozen, as he is treated as acting on the entity's behalf
He must be offered the chance to move his funds first
Only the company's accounts can be frozen
His account can be frozen only after a court order
quiz.explanation: SBP's FAQ 14 says a member of a designated or proscribed entity who works in it as a director or member falls within 'a person acting on behalf of' it, so his personal accounts are liable to be frozen. Prior notice is never given.

quiz.question: A screening alert shows a partial name match with a newly designated person, but key identifiers are missing. What do SBP's FAQs expect?
options: File a CTR and continue normal operations
Ignore it until all identifiers are available
Ask the customer to confirm his identity before acting
Place an immediate temporary freeze and inform SBP for verification with the Ministry of Interior focal point
quiz.explanation: FAQ 7 says a potential match leads to an immediate temporary freeze, with SBP passing it to the Ministry of Interior focal point for verification. Asking the customer first would give prior notice.

quiz.question: Which of these is permitted on an account frozen under TFS, according to Regulation 4?
options: Accepting deposits (credits) without changing the frozen status
Deducting routine bank charges
Allowing withdrawals for urgent family needs at the manager's discretion
Treating it as unclaimed after ten years
quiz.explanation: Regulation 4(13) allows credits into frozen accounts. Charges cannot be deducted unless specifically allowed, frozen accounts are not surrendered as unclaimed deposits, and withdrawals need a formal exemption.

quiz.question: A designated person has an exemption SRO allowing a fixed monthly withdrawal. Last month he took nothing; this month he asks for double. What should the bank do?
options: Allow double, since the total stays within the exemption
Ask MoFA to approve the extra amount by phone
Refuse both months, because exemptions lapse if unused
Allow only the monthly exempted amount, as cumulative withdrawals are not permitted
quiz.explanation: SBP's FAQ 4 says cumulative withdrawal is not allowed: only the exempted amount can be drawn each month. Charges and taxes must also stay within the exempted amount.

quiz.question: Which UN Security Council resolutions do SBP's FAQs cite as examples of proliferation-related sanctions regimes?
options: UNSCR 1718 and UNSCR 2231
UNSCR 1267 and UNSCR 1988
UNSCR 1325 and UNSCR 2178
UNSCR 1373 only
quiz.explanation: The FAQs use UNSCR 1718 and 2231 as examples of proliferation financing regimes, and UNSCR 1267 and 1988 as examples of terrorism-related regimes. UNSCR 1373 underlies domestic designations.

quiz.question: After due diligence, a frozen account turns out to belong to someone with the same name as a listed person, with a different CNIC and date of birth. What does Regulation 4 require?
options: Unfreeze after confirming no other freezing authority applies, and report the unfreezing to SBP
Unfreeze it and tell no one, as it was a mistake
Keep it frozen until the listed person is delisted
Ask NACTA to remove the customer's name from its list
quiz.explanation: Regulation 4(9)-(10) allows unfreezing for a verified false positive, but only after due diligence that no other blocking order applies, and the unfreezing must be reported to SBP.

quiz.question: An inward remittance from abroad gives only the originator's name, which partly matches a Fourth Schedule entry. The foreign bank cannot provide more data. What do SBP's FAQs say?
options: Always reject and freeze the beneficiary's account
Always execute, since foreign banks aren't bound by ATA lists
Decide to execute or reject under the bank's wire-transfer policies, and document the decision and its basis
Return it unprocessed with a message naming the list
quiz.explanation: FAQ 11 points to Regulation 11's risk-based policies for incomplete wire transfers. The bank decides under those procedures and documents the decision and its reasons. A message naming the list could tip off the parties.

sessions.title: The Bank's Programme: Compliance, Training, Board, Audit and Penalties
sessions.summary: Put it all together the way SBP inspects it: the compliance officer and the compliance function, the annual training programme under Regulation 13, the board's ultimate responsibility, independent audit, employee screening, and the sanctions SBP can impose under the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020.
objectives: Describe the compliance programme duties in sections 7F to 7H of the AML Act and SBP's Regulation 13
Build an annual AML/CFT/CPF training programme that meets Regulation 13, paragraphs 11 to 16
Explain the roles of the board, senior management, compliance and internal audit
Identify the sanctions SBP can impose and the factors it weighs under the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020

cards.title: The board wants answers
cards.setting: Board Risk Committee room, Karakoram Bank, Islamabad. 3:00 pm.

lines.text: Rashid Hayat, independent director. SBP inspectors arrive next month. I want to know, as a director, what I personally am answerable for.
The regulations put the ultimate responsibility for effective AML/CFT/CPF controls on the board. That's why you approve the IRAR and the policy.
And the training? Last year's attendance sheet looked thin, and nobody tested anything.
Regulation 13 wants an annual programme built on a formal needs assessment, with periodic testing. Online training and tests for front-end staff too.
Also, my branch ops managers ask why they can't approve their own branch's high-risk accounts. It would be quicker.
Final stage: the Council Chamber. Today we build the programme an inspector would sign off, and you'll be ready for the final boss.

cards.title: The pillars of a compliant programme

scenes.heading: Understand the risk
scenes.narration: Section 7F requires every reporting entity to identify, assess and understand its risks. For banks this is the board-approved internal risk assessment under Regulation 1.

scenes.heading: A compliance officer with clout
scenes.narration: Section 7G requires compliance arrangements that include a compliance officer at management level. Regulation 13 adds timely access to all customer records for the officer and their team.

scenes.heading: Policies that cover sanctions
scenes.narration: Section 7H requires policies and procedures for TFS duties. The board approves the policy, and senior management approves the procedures and SOPs.

scenes.heading: Trained, tested people
