scenes.narration: Regulation 13 requires an annual training programme from a formal needs assessment, covering everyone from sponsor shareholders to field staff, with periodic testing.

scenes.heading: Independent checking
scenes.narration: An independent, adequately resourced audit function regularly tests whether the policies and controls work. The board gets reliable management information to oversee it all.

cards.title: Who is answerable for what
cards.caption: Sources: AML Act s.7G; SBP Regulations 1(12)-(13), 5 and 13.

items.label: Board of directors
items.detail: Ultimate responsibility; approves IRAR and policy; needs reliable MIS.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Approves procedures; approves PEP and high-risk relationships.

items.label: Compliance officer
items.detail: Management-level; access to all records; runs monitoring and reporting.

items.label: Line management and branches
items.detail: Apply CDD, screening and escalation every day.

items.label: Internal audit
items.detail: Independent, resourced; tests whether it all works.

cards.title: Building the Annual Training Program (Regulation 13)
cards.prompt: Put the steps for Karakoram's annual AML/CFT/CPF training programme in order.
steps: Run a formal training needs assessment for the year
Design sessions for sponsor shareholders, the board, senior management, line management and field staff
Emphasise TFS for TF and PF and STR/CTR duties for staff responsible for oversight and preventive measures
Update content with the IRAR, NRA, international standards, regulatory changes and FMU, MoFA and NACTA guidance
Deliver it, including computer-based or online training for front-end staff
Test staff knowledge periodically and act where people fall short
Collect feedback and feed the results into next year's needs assessment

cards.question: Under Regulation 13, which group must Karakoram's annual AML/CFT/CPF training programme include?
options: Compliance staff only
Sponsor shareholders, the board, senior management, line management and field staff
Front-end staff only, because they meet customers
New joiners only, at induction
cards.explanation: Regulation 13(11) names sponsor shareholders, the board, senior management, line management and field staff. SBP's RBA guidelines add that training is ongoing, not a one-off at hiring.

cards.title: Training duties in detail (Regulation 13, paras 11-16)
cards.body:
- **Needs-based and annual.** The programme follows a **formal training needs assessment** each year.
- **Targeted emphasis.** Special focus goes to officials responsible for governance, oversight, supervision and monitoring of ML/TF/PF risk, and for preventive measures, including **TFS for TF and PF** and **STR/CTR**, as their jobs require.
- **Kept current.** Content reflects the IRAR, NRA updates, FATF and other international standards, regulatory and legal changes, and guidance from the **FMU, MoFA and NACTA**.
- **Skills, not just rules.** Training builds knowledge and analysis, including of the bank's RegTech systems and MIS.
- **Content for responsible staff.** New typologies and trends, plus their duties on **TFS, CDD and analysing out-of-pattern transactions and alerts** for possible STRs.
- **Tested.** Staff capability is **tested periodically**. For **front-end staff**, banks buy or build computer-based or online AML/CFT/CPF/TFS training and tests under a plan with clear timelines.
- **Outreach** to customers is encouraged.

cards.title: Regulation 13's internal controls
cards.prompt: Match each control in SBP's Regulation 13 to what it requires.

pairs.right: Compliance officers and their staff get timely access to all customer records.
AML/CFT/CPF duties are built into KPIs of responsible staff down the line.
Employees must not be given roles that conflict with each other.
The working strength of compliance is assessed every year and gaps fixed.
All staff, including outsourced staff, are screened against lists on an ongoing basis.
Apply the higher of Pakistan's or the host country's standard where the law permits.

cards.title: What's at stake
cards.setting: Board Risk Committee room, Islamabad. 3:40 pm.

lines.text: Suppose the inspectors find gaps. What can SBP actually do to us, and to me?

Under the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020, a lot: monetary penalties of up to 100 million rupees per violation, restrictions on business, warnings, suspension or removal of individuals, and directions to fix things.
The rules also list what SBP weighs: gravity, duration, compliance history, profits gained, remedial action, and whether it was negligent or wilful.
So a good remediation record actually counts.
It does. And if the bank took all reasonable steps and exercised due diligence, the rules say a sanction may not be imposed. That is what a real programme buys you.

cards.title: What's at stake: penalties in the law
cards.caption: Figures from the FMU's text of the AML Act (amended to September 2020) and SRO 950(I)/2020. Check for later amendments.

items.label: Max monetary penalty per violation, Sanctions Rules 2020
items.detail: Applied by SBP on its risk-based penalty scale.

items.label: Imprisonment for money laundering, AML Act s.4
items.detail: Plus a fine of up to PKR 25m and forfeiture.

items.label: Max fine for a legal person for money laundering, s.4(2)
items.detail: Guilty directors, officers or employees are punished too.

items.label: Max imprisonment for tipping off, s.34
items.detail: Or a fine of up to PKR 2m, or both.

items.label: Max imprisonment for wilful failure to file an STR, s.33
items.detail: Or a fine of up to PKR 0.5m, or both.

cards.title: The budget-cutting proposal
cards.situation: To save costs, the CEO proposes to the board: cancel this year's training needs assessment and reuse last year's slides, drop the online test for branch staff, and let branch operations managers approve high-risk accounts at their own branches 'to speed up onboarding'. Rashid asks for your view. What do you advise?

choices.text: Support it. SBP looks at outcomes, and the slides are still mostly accurate.
choices.outcome: Poor. Regulation 13 requires a formal needs assessment each year, current content and periodic testing. Branch managers approving their own high-risk accounts creates the conflicting roles Regulation 13(4)(b) forbids.

choices.text: Accept the cost cuts but keep the approval change under review.
choices.outcome: Partly reasonable on flexibility, but it still breaches the annual needs assessment and testing duties, and the conflicting-roles risk stays.

choices.text: Advise the board that all three changes conflict with Regulation 13, and propose cheaper ways to comply, such as in-house online modules and risk-based approval routing.
choices.outcome: Best. The board holds ultimate responsibility, so it needs a clear compliance view and a workable alternative. Regulation 13(16) expressly allows banks to build online training in-house.

choices.text: Keep training as it is but let branch managers approve high-risk accounts with a compliance review afterwards.
choices.outcome: Partly right on training, but a review after the event does not cure the conflict. EDD and PEP approvals belong with senior management before the relationship starts.

cards.back: Up to PKR 100 million per violation, under SBP's risk-based penalty scale.
Conditions, limits or restrictions on the bank's business or products.
Revocation of the licence or registration.
Written warning, temporary suspension or removal of managers who make decisions.
A statement of censure, warning or reprimand.
Remedial plans with deadlines, internal inquiries, or disciplinary action against directors and officers.
No sanction if the bank took all reasonable steps and exercised due diligence.

items.label: Assess risk (IRAR)
items.detail: Board-approved, NRA-informed, updated.

items.label: Set policy and procedures
items.detail: Board policy, management SOPs, proportionate to risk.

items.label: Train and implement
items.detail: Annual needs-based programme, tested.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Transaction monitoring, name screening, STR/CTR, TFS.

items.label: Audit independently
items.detail: Regular tests of effectiveness.

items.label: Report and remediate
items.detail: MIS to the board, then a time-bound action plan.

cards.question: Under Regulation 13, which arrangement for internal audit of AML/CFT/CPF is required?
options: A one-off review by the compliance officer before each SBP inspection
Testing done only by external auditors at year-end
Audit only of branches that filed STRs
An independent, adequately resourced function that regularly assesses effectiveness
cards.explanation: Regulation 13(5) requires an independent audit function, in line with the Code of Corporate Governance, that is adequately resourced and regularly assesses the effectiveness of AML/CFT/CPF policies, procedures and controls. Compliance cannot audit itself.

cards.title: Karakoram case: preparing for the SBP inspection
cards.body:
Ayesha's team runs a mock inspection. It finds:

- The IRAR was approved two years ago and ignores the **NRA 2023**. **Fix:** update it, take it to the board, attach a time-bound action plan.
- **Training** had no needs assessment and no test results for branch staff. **Fix:** run the TNA, launch online modules with tests for front-end staff, and record results in training MIS.
- **Rejected accounts** and revised risk ratings were not logged. **Fix:** start the register Regulation 13(3) requires.
- **Two vendors** and **one contractual employee** were never screened against the lists. **Fix:** re-screen and set up ongoing screening under Regulations 4(11) and 13(9).
- **Records** for accounts closed seven years ago were sent for destruction. **Fix:** stop it, because Regulation 8 requires ten years.

Rashid's committee approves the plan and asks for monthly MIS until every item is closed.

cards.title: Inspection-ready checklist
cards.body:
- Board-approved **IRAR**, current with the NRA, plus the action plan and progress.
- Board-approved **policy** and management-approved **SOPs**, including TFS.
- **Training**: TNA, annual programme, attendance and test results, online modules for front-end staff.
- **STR/CTR** files: analysis, decisions, goAML acknowledgements and timeliness.
- **TFS**: screening logs, list-update evidence, frozen-asset MIS, reports to SBP and the FMU.
- **Audit** reports and the status of fixes.
- **Records**: retention schedule matching Regulation 8.

cards.title: Stage five: what to remember
items: Sections 7F-7H: understand your risk, appoint a management-level compliance officer, train staff, and have policies for TFS.
Regulation 13: annual needs-based training for sponsors, board, management and field staff, kept current and tested periodically.
The board holds ultimate responsibility; senior management approves procedures and high-risk relationships; audit is independent.
No conflicting roles, AML duties in KPIs, a yearly check on compliance strength, and staff and vendors screened against lists.
SBP can impose penalties of up to PKR 100m per violation and act against individuals; a genuine programme and remediation matter.

cards.prompt: If an SBP inspector asked you tomorrow to show how your own AML/CFT/CPF training was chosen, delivered and tested, what evidence could you produce, and what is missing?

quiz.question: Section 7G of the AML Act requires a reporting entity's compliance arrangements to include what?
options: A separate AML subsidiary
An external AML consultant on retainer
A compliance officer approved by the FMU
A compliance officer at management level and training programmes
quiz.explanation: Section 7G requires compliance management arrangements, including a management-level compliance officer and training programmes, proportionate to ML/TF risk and size. The FMU does not approve compliance officers.

quiz.question: According to Regulation 13, what must come before the bank's Annual Training Program each year?
options: A board resolution naming each trainee
An FMU certification of trainers
An SBP pre-approval of the syllabus
A formal training needs assessment
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(11) requires the programme to be developed after a formal training needs assessment in AML/CFT/CPF, done annually. SBP does not pre-approve syllabuses.

quiz.question: Which statement about testing staff knowledge is consistent with Regulation 13?
options: SBP runs the tests for all bank staff
Testing is optional if attendance is recorded
Banks must test relevant staff periodically and provide online training and tests for front-end staff
Only compliance staff need to be tested
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(16) requires periodic testing of relevant staff and, for front-end staff, comprehensive computer-based or online training and tests, bought or built under a plan with timelines.

quiz.question: A bank's compliance head also runs the bank's largest branch and approves its high-risk accounts. Which Regulation 13 control does this most directly breach?
options: The duty to include ML/TF risks in ERM officers' KPIs
The duty to apply higher standards in overseas branches
The ban on assigning conflicting roles to employees
The requirement for online training of front-end staff
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(4)(b) prohibits conflicting roles. Running a business unit while approving its high-risk accounts undermines the independence compliance needs.

quiz.question: Under SBP's Regulation 1, who approves AML/CFT/CPF policies, and who approves controls and procedures?
options: SBP approves policies; the board approves procedures
Senior management approves both
The board approves policies; senior management approves controls and procedures
Compliance approves policies; audit approves procedures
quiz.explanation: Regulation 1(12) splits the approvals: the board approves policies, and senior management approves controls, procedures and preventive measures. The board keeps ultimate responsibility under Regulation 1(13).

quiz.question: SBP finds a breach at a bank that had a documented, well-run programme, took all reasonable steps and exercised due diligence. What do the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020 say?
options: The case must be referred to the FMU instead
The regulator may not impose a sanction where it is satisfied all reasonable steps were taken
Only the compliance officer may be sanctioned
A sanction must always be imposed for any breach
quiz.explanation: Rule 4(2) says the regulator may not sanction a person if it is satisfied the entity took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence. This rewards genuine programmes, not paper ones.

quiz.question: What is the maximum monetary penalty per violation that an AML/CFT regulatory authority can apply under the Sanctions Rules 2020?
options: PKR 500 million
PKR 25 million
PKR 2 million
PKR 100 million
quiz.explanation: Rule 6(1) caps monetary penalties at PKR 100 million per violation, under the regulator's risk-based scale. PKR 25 million is the individual fine cap for money laundering in section 4 of the AML Act.

quiz.question: An HR manager says contractual and outsourced staff don't need sanctions screening because they aren't permanent employees. What does Regulation 13 say?
options: All employees, permanent, contractual or outsourced, are screened against the lists on an ongoing basis
Screening is needed only at hiring, not afterwards
Only permanent staff with system access need screening
Outsourcing companies screen their own staff, so the bank need not
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(9) covers all employees, whether contractual, permanent or outsourced, and requires ongoing screening against designated and proscribed lists, with records. Regulation 4(11) also extends TFS compliance to vendors and employees.

quiz.question: Which of these must SBP-regulated entities keep under Regulation 13(3)?
options: Records of accounts rejected by compliance, risk ratings challenged or revised, and accounts closed for ML/TF/PF risk
Copies of every SBP circular
Staff attendance at all non-AML training
A list of all customers who complained to the Banking Mohtasib
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(3) requires banks to record rejected cases, cases where a business unit's risk rating was challenged or revised, and relationships closed because of ML/TF/PF risk. These are key evidence for inspectors.

quiz.question: Karakoram's overseas subsidiary is in a country whose AML rules are weaker than Pakistan's, and host law does not stop it applying stricter rules. What does Regulation 13 require?
options: Apply Pakistan's rules only to Pakistani customers
Close the subsidiary within 48 hours
Apply only the host country's rules
Apply the higher of the two standards to the subsidiary
quiz.explanation: Regulation 13(7) requires overseas branches and subsidiaries to apply the higher standard where host law permits. If host law prevents it, the head office must report to SBP under Regulation 13(8).

bank.question: Which authority is named in Schedule IV of the AML Act as the AML/CFT regulatory authority for entities licensed under laws SBP administers?
options: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
The State Bank of Pakistan
The Federal Board of Revenue
The Financial Monitoring Unit
bank.explanation: Schedule IV, part 1, names SBP for reporting entities licensed or regulated under laws it administers. SECP covers its own licensees and FBR covers certain DNFBPs. The FMU is the FIU, not a regulatory authority.

bank.question: The FMU's Director General has reasonable grounds to believe property is involved in money laundering and needs to act fast. What does section 6 of the AML Act allow?
options: An order freezing the property for up to fifteen days
An order confiscating the property permanently
An order freezing it for up to 180 days
An instruction to SBP to cancel the account holder's CNIC
bank.explanation: Section 6(6) lets the Director General order a freeze for a maximum of fifteen days, subject to NEC-sanctioned regulations. Longer attachment under section 8 needs an investigating officer and court permission.

bank.question: A trader receives cash he has reason to believe comes from smuggling and uses it to buy prize bonds in his wife's name. He has not been involved in the smuggling. Which statement is correct?
options: This is only a tax matter for the FBR
He may be guilty of money laundering, since acquiring or converting property while having reason to believe it is criminal is covered
He cannot be guilty because he did not commit the smuggling
He is guilty only if the smuggler is convicted first
bank.explanation: Section 3(a) covers anyone who acquires, converts or transfers property knowing or having reason to believe it is proceeds of crime, and Explanation II removes the need for a predicate conviction. Smuggling is a Schedule I predicate.

bank.question: A director of a bank knew that the bank's staff were knowingly processing proceeds of crime for a client and did nothing to stop it. Under the AML Act, what is the director's exposure?
options: He can be deemed guilty where the offence occurred with his consent, connivance or knowledge
None, because only the bank as a legal person is liable
Liability only if he personally signed the transactions
Only SBP's administrative sanctions, never criminal liability
bank.explanation: Section 37(2) makes directors and officers guilty where a legal person's offence happened with their consent, connivance or knowledge. Section 4(2) also lets guilty directors, officers and employees be punished. Signing the transactions is not required.

bank.question: Karakoram's risk team wants to know which predicate offences the NRA 2023 summary rated as 'Very High' ML threats, so it can tune monitoring. Which list is correct?
options: Terrorism, kidnapping, arms trafficking, piracy and counterfeiting
Insider trading, environmental crime, theft, robbery and forgery
Narcotics, human trafficking, fraud, cyber crime and extortion
Corruption and bribery, illegal MVTS/hundi/hawala, tax crimes, smuggling and cash smuggling
bank.explanation: The NRA 2023 summary rates corruption and bribery, illegal MVTS/hundi/hawala, tax crimes, smuggling and cash smuggling as 'Very High'. Narcotics, human trafficking, fraud and cyber crime were rated 'High', not 'Very High'.

bank.question: Which body hosts the FMU's database of STRs and CTRs and can share information with foreign FIUs under the AML Act?
options: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs
NACTA's financial wing
The FMU itself, under section 6(4)
SBP's Banking Inspection Department
bank.explanation: Section 6(4) gives the FMU the power to keep a database of STRs and CTRs and to cooperate with foreign FIUs. SBP supervises banks; MoFA and NACTA have sanctions and counter-terrorism roles.

bank.question: A branch manager argues that the bank should not report a customer because doing so would breach the customer's confidentiality agreement and expose the bank to a damages claim. What is the best response?
options: Confidentiality agreements take priority unless SBP orders disclosure
The bank should ask the customer's consent before filing
Only reports approved by the CEO are protected from lawsuits
The STR duty applies despite secrecy obligations, and good-faith reporting is protected from civil, criminal or disciplinary action
bank.explanation: Section 7(5) makes the reporting duty override secrecy rules in other laws or documents, and section 12 protects good-faith reporting. Asking the customer's consent would tip him off.

bank.question: Under the AML Act, what is the range of rigorous imprisonment for the offence of money laundering, in the FMU's text amended to September 2020?
options: Life imprisonment only
Up to three years
Not less than one year and up to ten years
Up to six months
bank.explanation: Section 4(1) sets rigorous imprisonment of not less than one year and up to ten years, plus a fine and forfeiture. Check for later amendments, as the quest notes.

bank.question: SBP's RBA guidelines describe a sequence for the bank's risk assessment. Which order is right?
options: Residual risk, then inherent risk, then controls
Inherent risk, then effectiveness of controls, then residual risk
Controls, then residual risk, then inherent risk
Customer risk only, then a board vote
bank.explanation: The guidelines describe measuring inherent risk without controls, then assessing control effectiveness, and arriving at residual (net) risk to compare against appetite.

bank.question: Karakoram's IRAR was approved by the board in 2022. The FMU later publishes the NRA 2023. What does Regulation 1 require?
options: Ask SBP whether an update is needed
Update only the customer risk scoring model
Nothing until the IRAR is three years old
Update the IRAR in light of the updated NRA and take it back to the board
bank.explanation: Regulation 1(7) requires the IRAR to be kept dynamic and updated when the NRA is updated, and Regulation 1(8) requires board approval. Waiting or updating only one model misses the point.

bank.question: A bank wants to open an account for a customer whose identity it has only partly verified, finishing the rest within the week. What does Regulation 2 allow?
options: Verification only if the customer is high risk
Verification before or during the establishment of the relationship; if CDD can't be completed, section 7D applies
No verification for customers introduced by staff
Verification at any time within a year
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(15) requires verification before, or during the course of, establishing the relationship. If it cannot be completed, section 7D requires the bank not to proceed, or to end the relationship, and to consider an STR.

bank.question: A company customer's ultimate owner is a foreign trust. Under Regulation 2, whose identity must the bank establish for the trust?
options: Only the person who signs the account opening form
Only the beneficiaries who receive money this year
Only the trustee company, as the legal owner
The settlor, the trustees, any protector, the beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and anyone else with ultimate effective control
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(11) requires the settlor, trustees, protector (if any), beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and any other natural person with ultimate effective control to be identified. Where any of them is a legal person, its own beneficial owner must be traced.

bank.question: Which situation requires EDD under Regulation 2(16), regardless of the customer's other characteristics?
options: A salaried customer with a credit card
A customer who prefers digital banking
A business relationship with persons from a country under the Counter Measures for High Risk Jurisdictions Rules 2020
A first-time customer from another province
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(16) lists higher-risk relationships, persons from countries under the 2020 counter-measures rules, and PEPs with their family members and close associates. The other cases are not automatic EDD triggers.

bank.question: An existing customer is appointed a provincial minister. What must the bank do under Regulation 5?
options: Obtain senior management approval to continue, establish source of wealth and funds, and apply enhanced monitoring
Close the account, because PEPs are prohibited
Nothing, because the relationship started before he became a PEP
Report him to the FMU as a matter of routine
bank.explanation: Regulation 5(1)(b) covers customers who become PEPs later: senior management must approve continuing the relationship. Source of wealth and funds, and enhanced monitoring, follow. PEP status alone is not suspicious and is not reported as routine.

bank.question: A customer's KYC file is missing a valid identity document because his CNIC has expired. What does Regulation 2 require?
options: Block debits after serving one month's prior notice until a valid document is provided and verified
Close the account immediately without notice
Freeze the account under TFS rules
Do nothing until the customer next visits
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(23) requires debit blocking of accounts without a valid identity document after one month's prior notice, lifted once a valid document is submitted and verified. TFS freezing is unrelated.

bank.question: Which of these is a permitted simplified due diligence measure under Regulation 2(18), where the IRAR identifies low risk?
options: Not screening the customer against sanctions lists
Verifying identity after the business relationship is established
Applying SDD to a customer under suspicion
Skipping identification of the customer entirely
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(18) lists measures such as verifying after the relationship is established, reduced monitoring and inferring purpose from transaction type. SDD never removes identification or screening and is barred when there is suspicion.

bank.question: A relationship manager onboards a company whose 'senior managing official' he records as the beneficial owner, without trying to find who owns or controls it. Why will an SBP inspector criticise this?
options: Beneficial owners need only be recorded for listed companies
The senior managing official is a last resort, used only if no person controls through ownership or other means
Senior managing officials can never be beneficial owners
The FMU must name the beneficial owner, not the bank
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(10) is a cascade: controlling ownership interest first, then control by other means, and only then the senior managing official. Jumping straight to the last step skips the required search.

bank.question: Regulation 2(17) lists possible EDD measures. Which of these is one of them?
options: Requiring the customer to bank only at the head office
Requiring the first payment to come from an account in the customer's name at a bank with similar CDD standards
Requiring a guarantee from the FMU
Requiring the customer to keep a minimum balance of PKR 1 million
bank.explanation: Regulation 2(17)(h) includes requiring the first payment to come through the customer's own account at a bank with similar CDD standards, where available. The other options are not in the regulation.

bank.question: Under the FMU's 2025 Regulations, what must a reporting entity examine before deciding that a transaction is suspicious?
options: The available facts, including background information and the possible purpose of the transaction
Only whether the customer is on a sanctions list
Only the teller's personal opinion of the customer
Only whether the amount exceeds the CTR threshold
bank.explanation: Regulation 4(1) requires examining the available facts, including background and possible purpose, against the section 7(1) test. Amount and sanctions status matter, but they are not the whole test.

bank.question: A bank suspects that an account is about to be emptied of laundered funds and wants the FMU to act urgently. What do the 2025 Regulations provide?
options: The bank may immediately inform the FMU's Director General in writing, with grounds, so a freezing order can be considered
The bank must ask the customer to keep the funds in place
The bank may freeze the account itself for 180 days
The bank must wait for an SBP direction
bank.explanation: Regulation 5 lets a reporting entity inform the Director General in writing, with the grounds, and the DG may order a freeze under section 6(6) of the Act. Banks cannot impose their own long freezes for ordinary suspicion.

bank.question: After filing an STR, the FMU asks the bank for the account opening form and six months of statements. Under the 2025 Regulations, what must the bank do?
options: Refuse unless the FMU obtains a court order
Provide all supporting documentation promptly
Send the documents only at the next quarterly review
Ask the customer's permission first
bank.explanation: Regulation 10(1) requires reporting entities to provide supporting documents and other information the FMU requires promptly. Asking the customer would tip him off, and no court order is needed.

bank.question: An analyst must choose goAML indicators for an STR based only on an LEA inquiry into a customer for tax evasion. What do the FMU's guidelines expect?
options: File a CTR instead of an STR
Select only the LEA inquiry indicator
Leave indicators blank, as they are optional
Select the LEA inquiry indicator plus another indicator for the underlying offence, and state whether information was shared with the LEA
bank.explanation: The guidelines say the LEA inquiry indicator does not express a suspicion alone, so a second indicator for the underlying offence (such as tax evasion) is needed. For LEA-based STRs, the 'action taken' field must say whether information was shared with the LEA.

bank.question: What does the FMU's guidance say about filing STR-F reports for one subject with many suspicious transactions?
options: File an STR-A instead whenever there are more than ten transactions
Combine all customers into one monthly STR-F
File a separate STR-F for every single transaction
File one STR-F per person or entity, adding all relevant transactions and linked parties
bank.explanation: The FMU's guidelines call for a separate STR-F for each person or entity, with multiple transactions added to it and linked parties included as needed. There is no need to file one report per transaction.

bank.question: A bank's group head office abroad asks the Pakistani branch for details of STRs it filed, for group risk management. Under section 34 and Regulation 15, which statement is most accurate?
options: STRs may never be mentioned to anyone, including group compliance
Any group entity may receive STR details without restriction
Only SBP can share STRs with the group
Sharing is possible only under proper group arrangements with safeguards against tipping off
bank.explanation: Section 34(1) allows disclosure where there are disclosure agreements for corporate groups under the regulations, and Regulation 15(4) requires group information-sharing policies with safeguards, including against tipping off. Unrestricted sharing is not allowed.

bank.question: A customer's account shows round-figure cash deposits just under the bank's internal sign-off level at several branches, then same-day transfers to unrelated individuals. The customer says it is 'family money'. Which combination best describes the bank's duties?
options: Treat it as possible structuring and layering, analyse it, and if suspicion forms file an STR-F promptly; CTRs are still due on any cash at or above the threshold
File CTRs only, since cash is involved
Close the account immediately and tell the customer why
Ignore it, since the customer gave an explanation
bank.explanation: Deposits kept below thresholds and moved straight on to unrelated parties are classic FMU red flags. A suspicion leads to a prompt STR-F, and CTRs are a separate, automatic duty. Explaining the closure would tip the customer off.

bank.question: Under Regulation 8, how must transaction records be kept?
options: Only in paper form, signed by the branch manager
So that individual transactions can be reconstructed, in a form admissible as evidence
As summary monthly totals only
Only for customers who have been reported
bank.explanation: Regulation 8(4) requires records detailed enough to reconstruct each transaction (nature, date, currency type and amount, account) and kept in paper, electronic or microfilm form admissible in court.

bank.question: Under the AML Act as amended in 2020, how promptly must an STR be filed?
options: Within one year of the suspicion
Only at the end of the financial year
Promptly
Within 30 days of the transaction
bank.explanation: The 2020 amendments changed the proviso to section 7(1) to require filing 'promptly', replacing an earlier fixed deadline. The FMU's 2025 Regulations repeat this for goAML filing.

bank.question: A bank receives a currency transaction exemption for a qualified business customer from the FMU's Director General. What must the bank do before the exemption period ends?
options: Review the customer at least 30 days before expiry and resubmit the request if needed
Ask SBP to extend the exemption
Nothing; exemptions renew automatically
File back-dated CTRs for the exempt period
bank.explanation: Regulation 8(2) of the 2025 Regulations requires a review of qualified business customers at least 30 days before the exemption expires, and resubmission if required. The bank must also tell the FMU promptly if the customer no longer qualifies.

bank.question: Under Regulation 4, whose funds must be frozen besides those of the designated or proscribed person?
options: Every relative of the listed person
Every customer from the same district
Entities they own or control, and those acting on their behalf or at their direction
Only joint account holders named on the SRO
bank.explanation: Regulation 4(1) and 4(7) extend duties to entities owned or controlled directly or indirectly, and to anyone acting on their behalf or at their direction. Relatives are not covered by family ties alone, as SBP's FAQ makes clear.

bank.question: A corporate customer's new authorised signatory matches a proscribed person on NACTA's list. The company itself is not listed. What does Regulation 4 require?
options: Nothing, because only the company is the customer
Remove the signatory and continue as normal without reporting
Treat it as a TFS concern: entity accounts must not have signatories, directors or owners linked to DPs or PPs, so freeze and report as applicable
Ask the company to confirm in writing that the signatory is not the listed person
bank.explanation: Regulation 4(4) requires banks to ensure that beneficial owners, directors, members, trustees and authorised signatories of entity accounts are not linked to DPs or PPs. A confirmed link triggers the freeze and reporting duties in Regulation 4(7).

bank.question: Which list should a bank use for freezing and unfreezing under the Fourth Schedule of the ATA, according to SBP's FAQs?
options: The UN Security Council consolidated list only
The FMU's goAML watchlist
NACTA's consolidated list of proscribed individuals
A commercial screening vendor's list only
bank.explanation: SBP's FAQ 10 points banks to NACTA's public consolidated list, which is updated when changes are made, with emails circulated to SBP-regulated entities. Vendor lists may supplement it but are not the official source.

bank.question: A designated person's account was frozen. He asks the bank to set off his overdue loan against the frozen balance 'to reduce his debt'. What do SBP's FAQs say?
options: Set-off is allowed because the bank benefits
Set-off is allowed if the customer signs a consent
Set-off is not allowed, since debits from frozen funds need permission under the relevant laws
Set-off is allowed after 48 hours
bank.explanation: FAQ 17 says set-off is not allowed: debits from frozen funds are prohibited unless permitted under the law. Loan repayments into the loan account, however, can still be received.

bank.question: A person claims his funds were frozen by mistake under the ATA because his name matches a proscribed person. Where does SBP's FAQ say he applies?
options: To the Federal Government under section 11O(4) of the ATA
To the FMU through goAML
To the Banking Mohtasib
To the bank's branch manager, who can unfreeze on the spot
bank.explanation: FAQ 19 says that for freezing after proscription under the ATA, the affected person applies to the Federal Government under section 11O(4), which can order the release of wrongly frozen property. The bank also unfreezes verified false positives after due diligence and reports to SBP.

bank.question: Under SBP's Regulation 4(11), TFS compliance must extend to which of the following?
options: Only customers with foreign remittances
Only staff in the compliance department
Customers only
Vendors, employees including outsourced staff, the board, owners and sponsor shareholders
bank.explanation: Regulation 4(11) extends TFS compliance to vendors, employees (permanent, contractual or outsourced), board members, owners and sponsor shareholders. Regulation 13(9) separately requires ongoing employee screening.

bank.question: What does SBP's FAQ say about how often the UNSC and ATA sanctions lists are updated?
options: Only after FATF plenary meetings
There is no fixed interval; lists change whenever additions, deletions or amendments are made
Quarterly, in line with SBP returns
Once a year, on 1 January
bank.explanation: FAQ 9 says there is no specific interval and that banks must apply all changes without delay. That is why screening databases must be updated continuously.

bank.question: A trade customer asks Karakoram to confirm an LC for 'industrial controllers' to a new consignee via a transhipment hub. One shipping-party name partly matches an entity on a UN proliferation-related list given effect by MoFA. What is the strongest response?
options: Proceed if the customer provides an end-user certificate
Proceed, because proliferation sanctions don't apply to trade finance
Reject the LC and tell the customer it hit a UN list
Halt processing, screen every party, treat a potential match as a temporary freeze with SBP verification, and escalate for EDD and a possible STR
bank.explanation: Regulation 4 applies TFS to persons designated under the UNSC Act, including proliferation regimes. Potential matches get a temporary freeze and verification through SBP. Telling the customer which list was hit risks tipping off, and paperwork alone does not clear a match.

bank.question: Regulation 13(12) requires training content to be updated in light of several sources. Which of these is one of them?
options: Customer satisfaction surveys
The bank's marketing calendar
Guidance and analysis issued by the FMU, MoFA and NACTA
Competitors' annual reports
bank.explanation: Regulation 13(12) lists emerging risks from the IRAR, NRA updates, international standards and best practice, regulatory and legal updates, and guidance and analysis from government, especially the FMU, MoFA and NACTA.

bank.question: SBP's RBA guidelines describe the qualities of effective AML/CFT training. Which set matches them?
options: High quality, obligatory for relevant staff, tailored by business line, effective, ongoing, complemented by updates, with feedback
Delivered once at hiring, with a signed acknowledgement
Focused on compliance staff only, with an annual test
Short, voluntary, generic, annual only, and untested
bank.explanation: The RBA guidelines list training that is high quality, obligatory, tailored, effective (for example, checked through tests), ongoing rather than one-off, complemented by information updates, and improved through formal feedback.

bank.question: Under Regulation 13(4)(c), what must a bank assess every year about its compliance function?
options: Whether the compliance officer holds a foreign certification
Its working strength, across all sub-divisions, fixing deficiencies as a priority
The number of STRs filed compared with other banks
Its contribution to branch profit
bank.explanation: Regulation 13(4)(c) requires an annual assessment of the working strength of the compliance function and all its sub-divisions, with deficiencies addressed on priority. STR counts alone do not measure adequacy.

bank.question: Which factor do the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020 list for the regulator to consider when setting a sanction?
options: The bank's market share in its home province
The number of branches in rural areas
Remedial measures the person took to address the cause of the contravention
Whether the CEO has met the regulator before
bank.explanation: Rule 4(3) lists gravity and duration, the need for a dissuasive and proportionate sanction, compliance history, financial strength, profits gained or losses avoided, remedial measures, and whether the breach was negligent or wilful.

bank.question: Under the Sanctions Rules 2020, against whom can an AML/CFT regulatory authority impose sanctions under section 6A(2)(h)?
options: Only the compliance officer
Only the reporting entity as a legal person
Any customer involved in the transaction
The reporting entity, its directors, senior management and officers in similar positions
bank.explanation: Rule 3(4) limits sanctions to the reporting entity and its directors, senior management and officers in similar positions. Customers are dealt with under criminal law, not these rules.

bank.question: SBP's 2016 guidelines on training bank employees, as summarised in its press release, asked banks to do what?
options: Outsource all training to SBP's training academy
Train only head office staff
Adopt a board-approved training policy based on needs assessment, with an annual training budget
Stop classroom training in favour of e-learning
bank.explanation: SBP's September 2016 press release summarised the guidelines: a board-approved training policy built on needs assessment, an annual board-approved budget, and attention to staff in remote and rural branches.

bank.question: An inspection finds Karakoram's IRAR is current, but the board receives only a one-page annual compliance summary and no data on STR timeliness, screening or training. Which requirement is most clearly unmet?
options: The board's duty to ensure adequate, reliable, periodic MIS for oversight under Regulation 1(13)
The duty to file CTRs within seven working days
The ban on numbered accounts
The requirement for Form-B notices
bank.explanation: Regulation 1(13) gives the board ultimate responsibility and requires it to ensure adequate, reliable and periodic MIS from senior management. An annual one-page summary does not allow effective oversight.

bank.question: The compliance officer finds that the business units are not giving her team access to customer files for alert reviews, claiming 'data protection'. Which provision supports her?
options: Section 11OO of the ATA on exemptions
Regulation 2(24) on dormant accounts
Section 7J of the AML Act on customer appeals
Regulation 13(2), which requires timely access to all customer records for compliance officers and their staff
bank.explanation: Regulation 13(2) requires compliance officers, and those assisting them, to have timely access to all customer records and relevant information. Data protection does not override this internal compliance access.
